title: The Order of an Element
short: The order of a mod n is the smallest k > 0 with aᵏ ≡ 1; it divides φ(n), and the powers of a repeat with that period.
trouble: Students take φ(n) as the order, but the order can be any divisor of φ(n): the order of 2 mod 7 is 3, not 6.

blocks.html: Euler's theorem says $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1$, so the powers of a unit $a$ eventually come back to 1. But often they come back sooner: mod 7, $2^{3} = 8 \equiv 1$, long before $2^{6}$. The first return time is the most useful single number about $a$.
Definition. If $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, the order of $a$ mod $n$, written $\operatorname{ord}_n(a)$, is the smallest $k > 0$ with $a^{k} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$.
Theorem. Let $k = \operatorname{ord}_n(a)$. Then $a^{m} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ exactly when $k \mid m$. In particular $k \mid \varphi(n)$, and the powers of $a$ repeat with period exactly $k$.

Divide $m$ by $k$: $m = kq + r$ with $0 \le r < k$. Then $a^{m} = (a^{k})^{q} a^{r} \equiv a^{r}$. If $a^{m} \equiv 1$, then $a^{r} \equiv 1$ with $r < k$; since $k$ is the smallest positive exponent that gives 1, $r$ must be $0$, so $k \mid m$. (Conversely $k \mid m$ clearly gives $a^{m} \equiv 1$.) Euler's theorem gives $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1$, so $k \mid \varphi(n)$.

blocks.name: nt-powers

opts.task: Find a base $a$ whose powers visit all six nonzero points before returning to 1.

blocks.cap: The powers of 2 mod 7 run $2, 4, 1$ and repeat: order 3, a divisor of $\varphi(7) = 6$. Bases 3 and 5 go all the way around.

blocks.title: By listing powers
steps: The first power that is 1 is the third.

blocks.title: Testing only divisors
steps: The order divides $\varphi(13) = 12$, so it is one of $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12$.

blocks.title: Order of a power
steps: $(2^{8})^{m} = 2^{8m} \equiv 1$ exactly when $12 \mid 8m$, that is, when $3 \mid 2m$, that is, when $3 \mid m$.
So the order is $3 = \dfrac{12}{\gcd(12, 8)}$. Check: $2^{8} = 256 \equiv 9$, and $9^{3} = 729 = 56 \cdot 13 + 1$.

blocks.html: The last example is a general rule: if $\operatorname{ord}_n(a) = k$, then $\operatorname{ord}_n(a^{j}) = \dfrac{k}{\gcd(k, j)}$.

Orders explain repeating decimals. The decimal of $\frac{1}{7} = 0.\overline{142857}$ repeats every 6 digits because $\operatorname{ord}_7(10) = 6$: the first $k$ with $7 \mid 10^{k} - 1$ is $k = 6$, since $999{,}999 = 7 \cdot 142{,}857$. In general, for $p \ne 2, 5$, the period of $\frac{1}{p}$ is $\operatorname{ord}_p(10)$, so it always divides $p - 1$.

Taking $\varphi(n)$ as the order. $\varphi(7) = 6$, but $\operatorname{ord}_7(2) = 3$: the order can be any divisor of $\varphi(n)$. Euler's theorem gives a multiple of the order, not the order itself. To find the order, test the divisors of $\varphi(n)$ in increasing order and stop at the first one that gives 1.
$\operatorname{ord}_n(a)$ is the first $k > 0$ with $a^{k} \equiv 1$. It divides $\varphi(n)$, and $a^{m} \equiv 1$ exactly when the order divides $m$.
